title: Mardi Gras! One month late
summary: Josh and Chuck record a topical episode on Mardi Gras timed to Fat Tuesday, released a month later. They open with tour dates (Vancouver and Portland, March 2020) and a shout-out to Doug Sassary and a New Orleans boil. They cover the origins of the word "carnival" and Mardi Gras, the French explorer Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville naming Point du Mardi Gras, early spontaneous street revelry and its rowdiness, the 1857 founding of the Mystic Krewe of Comus as the first modern parade, the 1872 introduction of the purple, green and gold colors (a Romanov legend they dismiss), king selection, and throws like doubloons, beads and moon pies. They discuss corporate sponsorship, the Zulu Social Aid and Pleasure Club and its blackface controversy, king cakes and the plastic baby, the Carnival season calendar tied to Easter, the super krewes, float reuse rules, and masks. The episode ends with a listener email about closing bedroom doors during a fire.

segments.title: Tour dates and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh announces March 2020 shows in Vancouver and Portland, then banter about recording Mardi Gras a month early and New Orleans hospitality. He shouts out Doug Sassary.

segments.title: Name of Carnival and Mardi Gras origins
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the word carnival and its Latin roots, the Mardi Gras season ending on Fat Tuesday before Ash Wednesday, and how Carnival in Brazil is the same festival. Chuck explains Lent and Ash Wednesday, and the pagan harvest roots of the celebration.

segments.title: Early history and Mobile connection
segments.summary: They describe the French explorer who named the area Point du Mardi Gras, the earlier celebrations in Mobile, and the New Orleans Mardi Gras parties after the city was founded. Early street revelry in the 1820s and 1830s became rowdy and violent, prompting city leaders to act.

segments.title: Krewes and the first modern parade
segments.summary: In 1857 the Mystic Krewe of Comus staged the first organized parade, after which krewes grew into well-funded charity organizations. The hosts describe anonymity, masks, and electing kings. The 1872 introduction of the purple, green, and gold colors and the Romanov legend, which they call untrue, are covered, along with the origin of throwing beads.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Brief mid-episode break; hosts mention Mardi Gras economic impact and the lack of a single corporate sponsor.

segments.title: Corporate sponsors, Zulu and king cake
segments.summary: The hosts note that krewes operate autonomously and some take corporate sponsorship. They discuss Endymion and Bud Light, and the Zulu Social Aid and Pleasure Club, its origins as a Jim Crow-era mutual aid society, and the blackface controversy. They then describe king cake, its plastic baby, and the baker practice of selling it with the baby in a separate package.
topics: Zulu Social Aid and Pleasure Club

segments.title: Calendar, super krewes, and float rules
segments.summary: They explain the Carnival season, which starts January 6 and runs through Fat Tuesday, with the date varying with Easter. They then describe super krewes with large membership and funding, Krewe of Bacchus breaking tradition by choosing a celebrity king, themes and rented floats, and the local rule limiting how often a float can pass through the business district.

segments.title: Moon pies and throws
segments.summary: The hosts describe throws such as doubloons and moon pies, which replaced Cracker Jack boxes after Mobile banned them, and the moon pie's history from the Chattanooga Bakery in 1917.

segments.title: Listener mail: close your door when you sleep
segments.summary: A research engineer named Mark writes about the Close Before You Doze campaign, which encourages residents to close bedroom doors at night to slow fire spread. Josh says he still sleeps with his door open.
